question:
You are a peer scientific reviewer for the One-Wave project. First follow this repository-reading discipline: distinguish Builds (engineering), One-Wave-Science (hypotheses/simulations/data/controls), and Bridge-Comand (transport/receipts); find README/index/map and dated canon/corrections/contracts before interpreting; follow references needed for claims; classify statements as established external ingredient, project hypothesis, simulation result, bench result, implementation evidence, or unresolved; for science inspect assumption/transformation contracts, controls/nulls, units, parameter freedom, provenance, uncertainty, residuals, held-out tests and validation status. Never claim to have read a repository file unless its contents were actually supplied/retrieved.

Known current science direction: One-Wave-Science is building a 24->1 modular simulation sandbox. It has an assumption/transformation contract with immutable RAW SOURCE -> SOURCE/UNITS -> ASSUMPTION -> TRANSFORMATION -> CONTROLS/NULLS -> RESULT -> RESIDUAL -> VALIDATION STATUS -> VERSIONED REFERENCE. Validation is PROPOSED -> CALIBRATED -> TESTING -> SUPPORTED/UNSUPPORTED/UNRESOLVED -> SUPERSEDED, and SUPPORTED is scoped, not universal proof. Public-data work includes CERN Open Data/CMS and LIGO/GWOSC metadata; raw data must remain separate from transforms. A current G-767 candidate uses a log2/octave coordinate u=log2(x/x0), n=floor(u), phi=u-n and explicitly still needs density-matched nulls, train/test separation, frozen x0, machine receipts and controls before interpretation. A related G-766 residual is r_mn=log2(fm/fn)-round(log2(fm/fn)). The broader project explores a One-Wave/lattice framework without assuming particles as fundamental; simulations include lattice/field/path/scale ideas. None of this is established physical proof.

Question: If you were joining this project specifically to ATTACK AND BUILD UP THE SCIENCE, where would you attack first? Pick the highest-leverage falsifiable target, not the most exciting claim. Explain (1) which repo files/contracts/data you would inspect next, (2) the weakest dependency or biggest confound, (3) the best discriminating test against a conventional/null explanation, (4) exact data/controls/metrics needed, (5) what result would weaken or kill the current hypothesis, (6) what result would only justify the next experiment rather than count as proof, and (7) the concrete next repo job you would implement. Be critical and constructive. Do not reward octave patterns unless they survive controls designed to manufacture/destroy those patterns. If you lack actual repository contents beyond this supplied context, explicitly identify what you still need to read.
